hello.title: Hello, Gleam!
hello.summary: Write your first Gleam program, print text with io.println and use modules from the standard library.
hello.lesson.0: Gleam is a friendly language with types. It runs on the Erlang virtual machine and in JavaScript. A Gleam program is made of **modules**: every `.gleam` file is one module. A program starts in a public function called `main`.
hello.lesson.2: Line by line: `import gleam/io` loads the module `gleam/io` from the standard library. After the import, you use it by its last part, `io`. `pub fn main()` defines a function: `fn` means function, `main` is its name and `pub` (public) means that code outside the module can call it. The code of the function goes between the braces `{` and `}`.
hello.lesson.4: `io.println` prints a **string** (a text) and then ends the line. A string goes in double quotes `"`. `io.print` prints a string but does not end the line. The lines of `main` run from top to bottom.
hello.lesson.6: Gleam checks your program before it runs. `io.println` only accepts a string, so `io.println(42)` does not compile. You will learn how to turn numbers into strings in the next unit.
hello.lesson.8: The standard library has many modules, for example `gleam/io` for printing and `gleam/string` for working with text. Write one `import` line for each module you need. `string.uppercase` writes a text in capital letters, and `string.reverse` turns it around.
hello.lesson.10: A line that starts with `//` is a **comment**. Gleam ignores it. Gleam also warns you when you import a module that you do not use.
hello.lesson.11: Gleam is case sensitive. Function names are written in lowercase with underscores, like `io.println`, so `io.Println` does not exist. Strings always use double quotes: `'Hi'` is not valid Gleam.
hello.card.1: `pub fn main() { … }` is where the program starts
hello-1.prompt: In which function does a Gleam program start?
hello-1.explain: Gleam starts the program in the public function `main`.
hello-2.explain: `io.print` does not end the line, so `morning` follows on the same line.

hello-5.explain: Module names are written with slashes and without quotes: `import gleam/io`.
hello-6.prompt: Complete the program so it runs and prints Ready.
hello-6.explain: `pub` makes the function public. `public` and `export` are not Gleam keywords.

hello-8.explain: The lines of `main` run from top to bottom. `io.print` does not end the line, so `ady` follows `Re` on the same line.

values.title: Values and types
values.summary: Name values with let and get to know the types Int, Float, String and Bool.
values.lesson.0: Every value in Gleam has a **type**. The basic types are `Int` (whole numbers like `7`), `Float` (numbers with a decimal point like `2.5`), `String` (text like `"hi"`) and `Bool` (`True` or `False`).
values.lesson.1: `let` gives a value a name, for example `let apples = 3`. Names are lowercase and use underscores between words, like `total_price`. `io.println` only prints strings, so `int.to_string` from the module `gleam/int` turns an `Int` into a `String`.
values.lesson.4: For `Int` you use `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` and `%`. The division `/` drops the remainder, and `%` gives the remainder. A `Float` has its own operators with a dot: `+.`, `-.`, `*.` and `/.`. `int.to_float` turns an `Int` into a `Float`, and `float.to_string` turns a `Float` into a `String`.
values.lesson.6: A `Bool` is `True` or `False`, always with a capital letter. You get one from a comparison: `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`. `&&` means "and", `||` means "or" and `!` means "not". `bool.to_string` turns a `Bool` into a `String`.
values.lesson.9: Gleam finds the types by itself, but you can write them after a colon: `let score: Int = 10`. A value never changes. You can create a new value with the same name, and from then on the name means the new value.
values.lesson.11: Long numbers are easier to read with underscores: `1_000_000` is one million. Dividing an `Int` by zero does not crash in Gleam: `7 / 0` gives `0`.
values.lesson.12: Gleam never mixes `Int` and `Float`. `1 + 2.5` and `1.0 + 2.0` do not compile. Use `+.` for floats and `int.to_float` to turn an `Int` into a `Float` first.
values.card.0: `let x = 5` gives a value a name
values.card.3: `int.to_string(n)` turns an Int into a String
values-1.explain: `/` on two `Int` values drops the remainder: 17 divided by 5 is 3, remainder 2.
values-3.explain: Floats need the operators with a dot, and both sides must be `Float`. `1` is an `Int`.
values-4.statement: After `let x = 1`, you can write `let x = x + 1` to create a new `x`.
values-4.explain: The old value does not change, but the name `x` now means the new value `2`.
values-5.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 10.
values-5.explain: `4 * 2` is `8`, and `8 + 2` is `10`. `+.` only works with floats.
values-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 42.
values-6.explain: `42` is an `Int`, and `int.to_string` turns it into the string `"42"` that `io.println` needs.
values-7.explain: `a > b` is `True`, but `b > 5` is `False`. With `&&` both must be `True`. Gleam writes `False` with a capital letter.
values-8.prompt: Build the line that gives the value 3.5 the name price.
values-8.explain: `let`, then the name, then `=` and the value. Gleam has no `var`.
values-9.prompt: Match the type or operator with its meaning.

values-11.explain: A name must exist before you use it: first `width`, then `height`, then `area`, and print at the end.
values-12.explain: In Gleam, dividing an `Int` by zero gives `0`. The program does not crash.
strings.title: Strings
strings.summary: Join strings, use special characters and work with text using the gleam/string module.
strings.lesson.0: A string is a text in double quotes. The operator `<>` joins two strings into a new string. You can join many strings in a row.
strings.lesson.2: `<>` only joins strings. To add a number to a text, turn it into a string first, for example with `int.to_string`.
strings.lesson.5: Some characters need a backslash `\` in a string: `\"` is a double quote, `\n` starts a new line and `\\` is one backslash.
strings.lesson.8: The module `gleam/string` has many functions for text. `string.length` counts the characters, `string.uppercase` and `string.lowercase` change the case, and `string.repeat` repeats a text a number of times.
strings.lesson.10: Some functions answer a question with a `Bool`: `string.contains`, `string.starts_with` and `string.ends_with`. `string.trim` removes spaces at both ends. `string.split` cuts a text into a list of parts, and `string.join` puts parts together with a separator.
strings.lesson.12: The functions do not change the old string. `string.uppercase(word)` gives a new string, and `word` stays the same.
strings.lesson.13: `+` does not join strings, and `"Age: " <> 36` does not compile because `36` is an `Int`. Use `<>` with strings only.
strings-1.explain: `<>` joins the three strings in order.
strings-4.explain: `+` only adds `Int` values. Strings are joined with `<>`.

strings-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints HELLO.

functions.title: Functions
functions.summary: Write your own functions, use labelled arguments, chain calls with the pipe |> and create anonymous functions.
functions.lesson.0: A function gives a name to some code. You write `fn`, the name, the parameters with their types in parentheses, `->` and the type of the result. The last expression in the braces is the result. Gleam has no `return` keyword.
functions.lesson.2: A function can have several parameters and several lines. Only the value of the last line is the result. You need `pub` only for `main` and for functions that other modules use.
functions.lesson.5: A parameter can have a **label** in front of its name. When you call the function, you write `label: value`, and the order of labelled arguments does not matter. Labels make calls easier to read.
functions.lesson.8: The **pipe** `|>` passes the value on its left as the first argument to the function on its right. `x |> f` means `f(x)`, and `x |> f(y)` means `f(x, y)`. With pipes you read the steps from top to bottom. `string.append(a, b)` puts `b` after `a`.
functions.lesson.11: `fn(x) { x + 3 }` is a function without a name. You can give it a name with `let` and call it, or pass it to another function. The type `fn(Int) -> Int` means a function that takes an `Int` and gives an `Int`.
functions.lesson.13: The types must match: `double("4")` does not compile, because `double` needs an `Int`. A function always gives back the value of its last expression.
functions.card.0: `fn add(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int { a + b }`
functions.card.1: The last expression is the result
functions.card.2: `fn f(name name: String)` is called with `f(name: "Ada")`

functions-4.explain: Gleam has no `return`. The last expression of the function is its result.

case.title: Pattern matching
case.summary: Make decisions with case expressions, patterns and guards.
case.lesson.0: Gleam has no `if` statement. To make decisions, you use `case`. It compares a value with **patterns** from top to bottom and runs the first branch that matches. Each branch is written `pattern -> result`.
case.lesson.2: The pattern `_` matches any value, so it catches everything else. Gleam checks that a `case` handles every possible value. Without the `_` branch, this code does not compile. A `case` is an expression: it gives a value.
case.lesson.4: For a yes or no decision, use `case` on a `Bool` with the branches `True` and `False`. You can give the result of a `case` a name with `let`.
case.lesson.7: A name in a pattern, like `x`, matches any value and gives it that name. A **guard** adds a condition with `if`: the branch `x if x < 0` only matches negative numbers. With `|` one branch can have several patterns.
case.lesson.10: The pattern `"Hi " <> name` matches every string that starts with `Hi ` and gives the rest the name `name`. You can also match several values at once: write them with commas after `case`, and use the same number of patterns in each branch.
case.lesson.12: The order of the branches matters: only the first branch that matches runs. Put the catch-all branch `_` at the end.
case.lesson.13: Gleam cannot check whether guards cover every value. A `case` with only guard branches, like `x if x < 0` and `x if x >= 0`, does not compile. End it with a `_` branch. Guards also cannot call functions.
case.card.3: `x if x < 0 ->` is a branch with a guard
case.card.4: `"a" | "b" ->` several patterns, `"Hi " <> rest ->` start of a string
case-1.explain: `n` is `2`, so the second branch matches.
case-3.explain: `-3` is not `0` and not greater than `0`, so only the last branch `_` matches.
case-4.statement: A `case` must handle every possible value, or the code does not compile.
case-4.explain: Gleam checks that every value matches a branch. A `_` branch at the end handles the rest.

lists.title: Lists
lists.summary: Store many values in a list and work with list.map, list.filter, list.fold and list patterns.
lists.lesson.0: A **list** holds many values of the same type in order: `[3, 1, 2]` is a `List(Int)`. The module `gleam/list` has functions for lists. `string.inspect` turns any value into a string that looks like Gleam code, so you can print a list.
lists.lesson.2: `[1, ..numbers]` makes a new list with `1` in front of the items of `numbers`. The old list does not change. `list.append` joins two lists.
lists.lesson.5: `list.map` calls a function for every item and gives a new list with the results. `list.filter` keeps only the items for which the function gives `True`.
lists.lesson.7: `list.fold` combines all items into one value. It takes the list, a start value and a function. The function gets the result so far (`acc`) and the next item. List functions work well with the pipe `|>`.
lists.lesson.10: In a `case`, the pattern `[]` matches the empty list, `[x]` a list with exactly one item, and `[first, ..rest]` the first item and a list with the rest. If you do not need the rest, write `[first, ..]`.
lists.lesson.12: Lists are made to go through the items in order. Putting an item in front with `[x, ..list]` is fast, adding at the end with `list.append` is slower.
lists.lesson.13: All items of a list have the same type. `[1, "two"]` does not compile.
lists-3.explain: `[1, ..xs]` makes a new list `ys`. The list `xs` does not change.
lists-4.statement: A list can hold an Int and a String at the same time, like `[1, "two"]`.
lists-4.explain: All items of a list have the same type, so `[1, "two"]` does not compile.

lists-5.explain: `list.filter` keeps the items where the function gives `True`. `list.map` would give a list of `Bool` values.

lists-6.explain: `[first, ..]` matches every list with at least one item. `[first]` only matches lists with exactly one item.

lists-7.explain: `list.map` calls the function for every item and gives the new list.

recursion.title: Recursion
recursion.summary: Repeat work with functions that call themselves, on numbers and on lists.
recursion.lesson.0: Gleam has no loops like `for` or `while`. To repeat something, a function calls itself. This is called **recursion**. A recursive function needs a **base case** that stops, and a recursive case that comes closer to the base case with each call.
recursion.lesson.2: `Nil` is the type of a function that gives back nothing useful, like `io.println`. Its only value is also written `Nil`. Braces `{ }` group several expressions into a block. The block runs them in order and gives the value of the last one.
recursion.lesson.5: Follow the calls: `factorial(3)` is `3 * factorial(2)`, which is `3 * 2 * factorial(1)`, which is `3 * 2 * 1 * factorial(0)`. The base case `0 -> 1` stops the calls, and the result is `6`.
recursion.lesson.7: Lists work the same way. The empty list `[]` is the base case. For `[first, ..rest]` you handle the first item and call the function again with the rest.
recursion.lesson.10: An **accumulator** is an extra parameter that carries the result so far. When the recursive call is the very last step, Gleam does not need extra memory for it. So this style works even for a million calls.
recursion.lesson.12: Functions like `list.map` and `list.fold` use recursion inside. When one of them fits your task, use it instead of writing the recursion yourself.
recursion.lesson.13: Without a base case, or when the calls do not come closer to it, the function calls itself forever and the program never finishes.
recursion.card.1: Base case: `0 -> 1` or `[] -> 0` stops the calls
recursion-2.explain: Each call adds 1 and skips one item with `_`. Three items give `3`.
recursion-3.prompt: Which line is the base case?
recursion-3.explain: The base case gives a result without calling the function again. Here this is `0 -> 1`.
recursion-4.statement: Gleam has a `for` loop to repeat code.
recursion-4.explain: Gleam has no loops. You repeat code with recursion or with functions like `list.map`.

recursion-5.explain: The sum of an empty list is `0`. With `1`, every sum would be one too big.

recursion-6.explain: Each call must come one step closer to the base case `0`, so the next call uses `n - 1`.

recursion-8.explain: Each call puts `n` in front of the rest: `[3, ..[2, ..[1, ..[]]]]`. The base case adds no `0`.

types.title: Custom types
types.summary: Define your own types and records, and handle missing values and errors with Result and Option.
types.lesson.0: With `type` you define your own type. You list its **variants**, and a value of the type is exactly one of them. Type names and variant names start with a capital letter. You handle the variants with `case`.
types.lesson.3: A variant can hold values in **fields** with labels. Such a value is called a **record**. You create it like a function call, `Person(name: "Ada", age: 36)`, and read a field with a dot: `ada.name`.
types.lesson.5: `Person(..ada, age: 37)` makes a copy of `ada` with a new `age`. The old record does not change. Different variants can hold different fields, and a pattern like `Circle(r)` gives the field a name.
types.lesson.8: Something that can fail gives a `Result`: `Ok(value)` when it works, or `Error(reason)` when it fails. `int.parse` turns a string into an `Int` and gives `Ok` with the number or `Error(Nil)`. You handle both cases with `case`.
types.lesson.10: An `Option` from `gleam/option` is a value that may be missing: `Some(value)` or `None`. With `import gleam/option.{type Option, None, Some}` you can write `Option`, `Some` and `None` without `option.` in front. `option.unwrap` gives the value or a default.
types.lesson.12: `result.unwrap` from `gleam/result` gives the value inside `Ok` or a default: `result.unwrap(int.parse("x"), 0)` gives `0`.
types.lesson.13: Names of types and variants start with a capital letter, like `Person` and `Some`. Names of values and functions start with a small letter.
types.card.0: `type Color { Red Green }` defines a custom type
types.card.1: `type P { P(name: String) }` is a record, `p.name` reads a field
